summary: GSS-API supports name-based authorization. This RFC introduces new APIs that extend its naming model so attributes of a name can be transferred between GSS-API peers.

plainLanguage.summary: A name tag can carry extra facts like role or group. This lets programs pass those facts along with the name.

questions: how to get name attributes in gss-api
what is a gss-api name attribute
what is the difference between authenticated and asserted attributes
subtitle: New GSS-API calls that let applications read, set and export attributes of a name, such as group membership, for authorization.

tldr.problem: The GSS-API naming model is simple and gives applications little beyond a name, yet applications often want attributes of the peer, such as authorization data, to make access decisions.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC models GSS names as having attributes, marks each as authenticated or merely asserted, names attributes with space-separated, URI-prefixed strings, and adds functions to inspect, get, set, delete and export them.
tldr.outcome: Applications can build portable access control on name attributes, but asserted attributes must not be used for security decisions and local policy decides what an authenticated attribute means.

today: RFC 6680 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It extends the GSS-API of RFC 2743.

sections.title: Why Names Need Attributes
sections.content:
RFC 6680 extends the Generic Security Service API (GSS-API, RFC 2743) and its C-bindings (RFC 2744) to overcome limits in the GSS-API naming architecture described in RFC 4768. The goal is to make information modeled as name attributes available to applications, for instance so they can make authorization decisions. Kerberos V authorization data elements are one example.

In the model, GSS names have attributes. An attribute may be authenticated (such as an X.509 attribute certificate or a signed SAML attribute assertion) or may be set on a name locally to assert it during credential acquisition or security context exchange. Attribute values are network representations, for example the octets of an X.509 certificate extension. A function is provided to obtain language- or platform-specific objects for names and attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: A name tag usually shows only a name. This adds room for extra facts on the tag, like which team you are on, so a program can decide what you may do.

sections.title: Authenticated and Asserted Attributes
sections.content:
An attribute is authenticated if and only if a secure association exists between the attribute and its values and the trusted source of the peer credential. Examples are the signed part of an X.509 certificate or AD-KDCIssued authorization data in Kerberos V tickets, provided the signatures were verified. An unauthenticated attribute is called asserted.

Authenticated does not mean the attribute is true, or that the credential source was allowed to assert it. Those conclusions SHOULD come from applying local policy. The RFC also says name attributes and values should be offered in canonical network encodings so applications can build portable access control lists.
sections.plainLanguage: A fact on a tag is authenticated if a trusted person stamped it. An asserted fact is one the wearer wrote on themselves, so you should not rely on it for anything important.

sections.title: Naming Contexts and Local Attributes
sections.content:
The same information can mean different things in different contexts. In an enterprise Kerberos deployment a Key Distribution Center typically may state anything about principals in its realm, including group membership. In a federated SAML environment the identity provider is usually in another organization, so the groups or entitlements it may assert must be filtered by the acceptor's and federation's policy. Even the role of a credential issuer matters: with PKINIT, a KDC might fully trust a certificate, or might only authorize a hash of it and so only state that the certificate was used. Encoding matters too, since an ASCII or UTF-8 email address is not the same as a DER email address in a certificate.

Therefore attributes with different contexts MUST have different names, and several attribute names will exist for the same basic information. To use local knowledge, the extensions also support local attributes, such as an implementation-defined email address attribute. These trade interoperability for usability: using a local attribute requires knowing the local implementation, while a standard attribute needs more policy and validation logic in the application. The RFC says both options are needed.
sections.plainLanguage: A fact like an email address can mean different things depending on who vouched for it. So the same fact written in two ways gets two different labels.

sections.title: How Attribute Names Are Written
sections.content:
Attribute names are OCTET STRING values and MUST support multiple components, where the more significant components define the meaning of the less significant ones. The first space (ASCII 0x20) separates the primary component, the prefix, from the rest of the name. If the primary component contains a colon, it is a URI. Otherwise the attribute is a local attribute, meaningful to the GSS-API implementation or the application configuration. Local names containing an at sign are reserved for future allocation by the IETF.

Because names are split at the first space, a mechanism that passes through a raw attribute it does not understand could create ambiguity. So a mechanism MUST always prefix raw name attributes with a prefix reflecting their context. Local names controlled by an administrator or a sufficiently trusted part of the platform need no context prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: Each fact has a label. The first word of the label tells you which family it comes from, and the rest says which exact fact it is.

sections.title: The New API Functions
sections.content:
Six new functions are defined, each with abstract and C-binding forms. GSS_Display_name_ext() displays a name using a given name syntax and may fail, because mapping can be inexact or lossy. GSS_Inquire_name() returns the set of a name's attributes and whether it is a Mechanism Name, and for which mechanism.

GSS_Get_name_attribute() returns the values of an attribute along with two flags: authenticated and complete. The complete flag says the values are a full set; in the federated case, where several peers may each hold some attributes, it may be highly dangerous and SHOULD NOT be used. In C, one call returns one value, and the more parameter must be -1 on the first call.

GSS_Set_name_attribute() sets values. On a Mechanism Name it MUST fail if the mechanism does not recognize the attribute. On a name that is not a Mechanism Name it may succeed, but later credential acquisition then MUST fail for mechanisms that do not understand the attributes. So all name attributes are locally critical. GSS_Delete_name_attribute() removes an attribute but MUST NOT allow deleting negative authenticated attributes, returning GSS_S_UNAUTHORIZED.

GSS_Export_name_composite() outputs a token, for inter-process use only, that keeps attribute information including the authenticated and complete flags, unlike GSS_Export_name(). Its tokens MUST start with the two-octet token ID hex 04 02. Implementations of SET OF OCTET STRING MUST preserve order, and the buffer set functions come from GFD.024.
sections.plainLanguage: There are new buttons: list the facts on a tag, read a fact, write a fact, erase a fact, and save the whole tag with its facts to pass to another program.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
IANA registered a new name-type OID in the "SMI Security for Name System Designators Codes (nametypes)" registry: 6, gss-composite-export, with absolute OID 1.3.6.1.5.6.6. This is the OID for GSS_C_NT_COMPOSITE_EXPORT.

The RFC also creates a namespace of GSS-API name attributes. Because attributes are named by URIs, no single authority is technically needed. Future experience may call for an IANA registry of URNs for IETF-specified attributes, but the RFC gives no further guidance.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of name types got one new entry, and facts are named with web-style addresses so anyone can make new ones.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Name attributes are meant to drive authorization decisions or personalization, so an application's security may depend critically on them. Asserted attributes MUST NOT be used where they have security implications, such as authorization, because the peer can easily control them.

Authenticated only means a trusted third party, rather than the peer itself, asserted the attribute. It does not mean the content is true; extra meaning comes from policy. For example, a mail attribute might come from an authoritative email system in one deployment and be freely editable by users in another, and be authenticated in both through signed SAML assertions.

When a mechanism gives no permanent unique identity, such as anonymous Kerberos, naming extensions may supply a permanent unique identity attribute, which can be globally unique, unique within the issuer's namespace, or directed per acceptor. SAML offers constructs for this, such as a persistent NameID format.
sections.plainLanguage: Never trust a fact someone wrote on their own tag when it matters. Trust a fact only if a trusted person stamped it, and even then decide for yourself what it means.

items.title: GSS_Display_name_ext
items.text: Show a name in a given name syntax; may be lossy.

items.title: GSS_Inquire_name
items.text: List a name's attributes and whether it is a Mechanism Name.

items.title: GSS_Get_name_attribute
items.text: Read values plus authenticated and complete flags.

items.title: GSS_Set_name_attribute
items.text: Add values to an attribute on a name.

items.title: GSS_Delete_name_attribute
items.text: Remove an attribute; negative authenticated ones are protected.

items.title: GSS_Export_name_composite
items.text: Export a name with its attributes for inter-process use.
